title: Clay closes new round at $7 billion pre-money, more than doubling its January mark
subtitle: The AI go-to-market platform is now valued at more than seven times its August 2025 price, with Wellington leading the latest round.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Clay, the New York-based AI go-to-market platform, is raising a new round at a $7 billion pre-money valuation led by Wellington, Axios reported on August 31. The mark is up from a $5 billion valuation set in a January 2026 employee tender led by DST and a $3.1 billion post-money in August 2025 after a $100 million Series C led by CapitalG. Clay was founded in 2017 and now serves more than 10,000 customers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Cursor. The platform combines AI agents, data enrichment, and intent signals into a single workflow layer for outbound sales and marketing.

The number is striking because Clay is not a foundation-model company — it is a workflow layer built on top of models other companies train. That distinction used to matter enormously to venture pricing, with the assumption that application-layer AI would compress into thin margins as models commoditized. Clay's trajectory argues the opposite: when the underlying models get cheaper and better, the software that decides what to ask them, and what to do with the answer, captures more of the value, not less. A 2.3x price jump in seven months, with real ARR growth underneath it, is the market pricing that argument in.

The pattern is not unique to Clay. Cursor, Perplexity, Harvey, and a small cluster of workflow-layer AI companies have all seen their valuations reset upward through 2026 while the foundation labs consolidate around a handful of frontier models. The bet public investors like Wellington are making here is that go-to-market — sales prospecting, outreach, deal orchestration — is one of the few enterprise workflows where AI agents can be trusted to run largely unsupervised, because the cost of a bad email is low and the cost of a good one is high.

Takeaway for learners: a valuation on its own is not a signal about a product's quality. It is a signal about what class of AI company the market currently rewards. Watch which layer of the stack is repricing — foundation models, agent orchestration, workflow tools, vertical applications — because that is where capital is betting the durable margins will land. And if you are choosing where to build a career, notice that the workflow layer is currently absorbing more of that capital than the model layer, which is closer to a two-horse race than most reporting suggests.
